clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: For each clinical group, deviations were summarized by computing the proportion of subjects with extreme deviations (Z>2 or Z<-2) in each region and comparing to matched controls from the same sites. Classical case-control comparisons were performed on both raw cortical thickness/subcortical volumes and on deviation scores using mass-univariate t-tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction (p<0.05). Results demonstrated that z-statistics derived from normative deviations provided stronger case-control effects than raw data for most diagnostic groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Normative models explained up to 80% of variance out-of-sample across cortical and subcortical regions, successfully captured diverse developmental trajectories, and when applied to transdiagnostic psychiatric cohorts, revealed widespread individual variability in deviation patterns and provided stronger case-control effects than raw data for most diagnostic groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The normative models fit well across the cortex and subcortex, explaining up to 80% of variance out-of-sample with similar performance between the full test set and manually quality-checked subset (N=24,354). Models successfully mapped diverse lifespan trajectories of different brain areas, aligning with known patterns of development and aging. When applied to the transdiagnostic psychiatric sample (N=1985 across 6 disorders), the models revealed considerable individual variability and heterogeneity in deviation patterns - not all individuals deviated in the same regions and different disorders showed different characteristic patterns. Extreme deviation summaries (Figure 2B-C) showed disorder-specific regional patterns. Case-control comparisons (Figure 2D) demonstrated that for most diagnostic groups, z-statistics derived from normative deviations provided stronger case-control effects than analyses on raw cortical thickness data. The individual-level deviation maps provide complementary information to group effects, demonstrating the value of normative modeling for quantifying clinically relevant information at the individual level. Transfer validation to 6 new OpenNeuro sites (N=546) demonstrated successful model generalizability.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Sampling bias from aggregating existing data predominantly from WEIRD societies (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic); UK Biobank contributes 59% of sample; race, education, and socioeconomic variables not fully available; semi-automated QC for full sample does not guarantee quality; FreeSurfer not adjusted for very young ages (2-7 years); models represent first step requiring augmentation with more diverse data, different features, and modeling advances
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: In order to provide coverage of the lifespan the curated data set is based on aggregating existing data, meaning there is unavoidable sampling bias. Race, education, and socioeconomic variables were not fully available for all included data sets, however, given that data were compiled from research studies, they are likely samples drawn predominantly from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies (Henrich et al., 2010) and future work should account for these factors. The sampling bias of UKBiobank (Fry et al., 2017) is especially important for users to consider as UKBiobank data contributes 59% of the full sample... Second, we have relied on semi-automated quality control (QC) for the full sample which-despite a conservative choice of inclusion threshold-does not guarantee either that low-quality data were excluded or that the data were excluded are definitively excluded because of artifacts... Also, Freesurfer was not adjusted for the very young age ranges (2-7 yo) thus caution should be used when interpreting the model on new data in this age range. Finally, although the models presented in this study are comprehensive, they are only the first step, and we will augment our repository with more diverse data, different features, and modeling advances as these become available

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Transfer learning procedure developed for applying pretrained models to new sites not in training set; involves applying warp parameters from training data to new data, adjusting mean/variance in latent Gaussian space; demonstrated on 6 OpenNeuro sites (N=546); models, code, and documentation shared via GitHub and Zenodo; Google Colab notebooks provided for easy access without local installation; interactive online visualization tool created for exploring evaluation metrics across test sets

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a landmark reference cohort study providing pretrained normative models for 188 brain regions (cortical thickness and subcortical volume) spanning ages 2-100. The study represents one of the largest normative modeling efforts in neuroimaging. UK Biobank contributes 59% of the full sample (approximately 34,714 subjects), which is important for users to consider regarding sampling characteristics. The manually quality-checked subset (mQC, N=24,354) includes data from 59 sites and provides a gold-standard validation. The study emphasizes the importance of using 'reference cohort' terminology over 'normative model' to avoid implications of normal vs. abnormal brains. Sex-stratified models were also estimated, confirming that sex effects are adequately captured by a global offset. The paper notes that Freesurfer was not run by the authors for UK Biobank data. Clinical validation demonstrates transdiagnostic applicability across ADHD, ASD, EP, SZ, BD, and MDD. All pretrained models, transfer code, and visualization tools are made openly available to facilitate community use.
